newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman poised to win last election battle.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman poised to win last election battle.

text.p: President Franjo Tudjman, fighting what is almost certainly his last election battle, is expected to romp home on Sunday with a strong mandate to push Croatia towards the West and finally shake off the legacy of its communist Yugoslav past.

But the 75-year-old former general faces a race against time if he wants to go down in history as the man who led Croatia into Western Europe -- he is reported to be ill with cancer and is not expected to live out his full term of office.
Viewed by the West as a key player in the struggling peace process in former Yugoslavia, Tudjman is not likely to benefit from much of a honeymoon period if he wins.
And he will have to weigh the demands of the West against the fears of a public still feeling the effects of war.
Recent unprecedented pressure from the United States and its allies looks set to continue until he tightens up his record on human rights and loosens his grip on the media.
His opponents in the presidential polls, both of whom have been attacked and harassed during the campaign, face a hopeless battle to oust him.
They have complained about Tudjman's unequalled access to state-run television, from which most Croatians get their daily news, and the partiality of the state electoral commission.
Vlado Gotovac, a philosopher running for the Social Liberal party, asked for the vote to be postponed after he was attacked at a rally and had to stop campaigning. His request was denied.

Zdravko Tomac of the Social Democratic party, the former communists, was the only contestant not allowed to address a rally in Zagreb's main square. "I am therefore not an equal candidate," he told reporters.

Observers expect Tudjman to win outright in the first round with 60-70 percent of the vote. It will be his second full term of office if he wins, though he was called president after assuming the role when Croatia won independence in 1991. He was later officially elected to the position in August 1992.
He has made enormous changes to a country which regards itself as part of central Europe and refuses to be labelled as Balkan -- a region it views as backward and corrupt.
He presided over an economic reform programme launched in October 1993 which stopped rampant inflation and stabilised the currency, leading foreign investment and domestic growth.
The peace process in former Yugoslavia has gone less smoothly. Tudjman's cooperation is vital if the 1995 Dayton peace treaty which ended the Bosnian war is to stick, and he has to tread carefully.
In order not to endanger vital international loans and aid needed for reconstruction, Tudjman has to meet the demands of Western powers, yet he cannot afford to alienate his public.

He is believed to have made slow progress in complying with the international war crimes tribunal in The Hague and not to have used his influence on Bosnian Croats to support Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation, forged by U.S. diplomacy in 1994.

Yet some diplomats say he has moved faster on other issues than Croatians want. "(The opposition) took the line last August when he made peace with Belgrade -- far too far and far too fast," one said.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright toured the area this month and publicly berated Tudjman and other ministers, telling him he had a "moral duty" to provide leadership.

"We believe that Croatia's future lies in the democratic community we are building. We hold Croatia to the standards of that community, not to the standards of this region's autocratic and violent past," she told a news conference.
The fact that the West has shown its impatience with Tudjman is likely to win him more votes from Croats who believe they are being unfairly victimised.
Even if Tudjman does make progress on key issues, Croatia's dreams of joining the European Union and other Western institutions are still a long way from being fulfilled.
"I'd have thought we are talking well into the next century before we're talking about EU membership," one diplomat said.
